notes.subject: language
notes.text: The only big Latin American country not writing Spanish: look for -ão endings, lh and nh, instead of -ón, ll and ñ.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: White plates with a blue stripe on top since 2018 (plain white before); red plates for commercial vehicles.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Soil is distinctly red nearly everywhere, light pink in Mato Grosso to deep maroon by the Paraná; not in the northeast or most of the far south.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Rectangular concrete poles with long slots at the bottom that look like a ladder, and small holes near the top.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road sign backs are painted black.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are yellow on black, unlike most of South America where they are black on yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue road markers show the road number and kilometre.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Double yellow centre lines with white edge lines; a single dashed yellow line also occurs.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Kerbs are often painted white.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Many houses have orange tiled roofs.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Transparent satellite dishes are, within Latin America, practically unique to this country.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Blue Fortlev water tanks are common on roofs.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Generation 3 is a white car with a stubby coiled antenna or no antenna at all.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: Generation 4 smallcam coverage exists here, along with Peru, Uruguay and Argentina.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Dry soil, shrubs and succulents in the northeast; still recognisable when rains turn them green.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Small grassy hills with scattered trees; roads ride the hills rather than going around them.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Open grassy plains with thin tufted grass and big distant mountains.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Lush green fields, hilly or flat; the far south can resemble Uruguay.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rolling grassy hills in Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, with rocky mountains in the last.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Paraná pines have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the tips; found in the southern states.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Carnaúba palms with fan-shaped leaves and a spiky lower trunk, common in Ceará, Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Açaí palms have thin trunks and drooping leaflets, mostly near Belém and across the Amazon.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in São Paulo state.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Coffee is most common in Minas Gerais.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Soybean fields are most common in Mato Grosso, Paraná and Goiás.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round concrete poles are common across the south, especially São Paulo.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wooden poles are most often seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas and Rio de Janeiro.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Smooth cone-topped "pencil" poles and Γ-shaped poles with electricity boxes are common in Rio de Janeiro.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Long yellow pole paint with a black code that starts with a letter appears in Bahia and Pernambuco.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Long yellow pole paint with a black code that always starts with a number marks Goiás.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Most poles in Maranhão have a small beige plate with numbers built into the concrete.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Poles at intersections in Paraná are sometimes painted with the street name.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Brown mushroom-shaped insulators appear only in Pernambuco; white ones in Bahia.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Spherical or cone-shaped "lollipop" insulators on a rod are common in Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba and Pernambuco.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Dark brown insulators with grey bases are almost exclusive to Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Lamp arms curved along their whole length are seen only in Rio de Janeiro.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: São Paulo has far more divided highways than any other state.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and Rio Grande do Sul.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, have houses with a vaguely German look.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Wooden houses on stilts are very common in Acre.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Round clay nests of the oven bird sit atop utility poles across the south.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Red gravel often lines the road edges in Piauí.
